# Network Estimation and Visualization with Nestimate + cograph

## 1 Introduction

**Nestimate** is a general-purpose network estimation package. It
provides a unified
[`build_network()`](https://rdrr.io/pkg/Nestimate/man/build_network.html)
interface that accepts raw sequence data and constructs networks using
multiple methods: transition probabilities, partial correlations,
regularized networks (GLASSO), co-occurrence, and more. The result is a
`netobject` that works directly with cograph’s
[`splot()`](http://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/splot.md) — no
conversion needed.

Beyond estimation, Nestimate provides bootstrap stability analysis,
permutation-based group comparisons, higher-order network construction
(HON, HYPA), and motif analysis. All output objects dispatch through
[`splot()`](http://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/splot.md)
automatically.

## 2 Data

We use `group_regulation_long` — a long-format dataset of 9
collaborative regulation behaviors coded across student groups, with
achievement group labels (High vs Low).

``` r

data("group_regulation_long")
head(group_regulation_long)
```

## 3 Estimating Networks

[`build_network()`](https://rdrr.io/pkg/Nestimate/man/build_network.html)
estimates a network from raw data. The `method` argument selects the
estimator.

``` r

net <- build_network(group_regulation_long,
  action = "Action", actor = "Actor", method = "relative")
net
```

[`splot()`](http://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/splot.md) renders the
`netobject` directly:

``` r

splot(net)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 1: Collaborative regulation — relative transition probabilities

One line builds different network types:

``` r

build_network(group_regulation_long, action = "Action", actor = "Actor", method = "frequency")
build_network(group_regulation_long, action = "Action", actor = "Actor", method = "attention")
build_network(group_regulation_long, action = "Action", actor = "Actor", method = "co_occurrence")
build_network(group_regulation_long, action = "Action", actor = "Actor", method = "glasso")
build_network(group_regulation, method = "pcor")
```

## 4 Bootstrap Stability

[`bootstrap_network()`](https://rdrr.io/pkg/Nestimate/man/bootstrap_network.html)
resamples the data and refits the model at each iteration, identifying
which edges are stable and which are sampling artifacts.

``` r

set.seed(265)
boot <- bootstrap_network(net, iter = 1000)
boot
```

      Edge                   Mean     95% CI          p
      -----------------------------------------------
      cohesion → consensus   0.498  [0.474, 0.521]  ***
      adapt → consensus    0.478  [0.430, 0.523]  ***
      synthesis → consensus   0.466  [0.427, 0.507]  ***
      consensus → plan     0.396  [0.383, 0.407]  ***
      monitor → discuss    0.375  [0.351, 0.401]  ***
      ... and 46 more significant edges

    Bootstrap Network  [Transition Network (relative) | directed]
      Iterations : 1000  |  Nodes : 9
      Edges      : 47 significant / 71 total
      CI         : 95%  |  Inference: stability  |  CR [0.75, 1.25]

### 4.1 Network plots

Significant edges appear solid; non-significant edges appear dashed
grey.

``` r

splot(boot)
```

``` r

splot(boot, display = "significant")
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 3: Significant edges only

``` r

splot(boot, show_stars = TRUE)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)


### 4.2 Forest plots

Forest plots show edge weights and confidence intervals in a compact
format. Three layouts are available:


``` r

```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 7: Circular forest plot

``` r

plot_bootstrap_forest(boot, layout = "grouped")
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 8: Grouped by source node

## 5 Group Networks

Pass `group =` to
[`build_network()`](https://rdrr.io/pkg/Nestimate/man/build_network.html)
to estimate a separate network per group.
[`splot()`](http://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/splot.md) renders all
groups in an automatic grid.

``` r

grp_net <- build_network(group_regulation_long, method = "relative",
  action = "Action", actor = "Actor", time = "Time", group = "Achiever")
names(grp_net)
```

    [1] "High" "Low" 

``` r

splot(grp_net)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 9: High vs Low achievers on a common weight scale

`common_scale = TRUE` (default) makes edge widths directly comparable
across panels:

``` r

splot(grp_net, common_scale = FALSE)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 10: Each group on its own scale

## 6 Permutation Testing

[`permutation_test()`](https://rdrr.io/pkg/Nestimate/man/permutation_test.html)
tests whether each edge differs significantly between two groups.

``` r

set.seed(265)
perm <- Nestimate::permutation_test(grp_net$High, grp_net$Low, iter = 1000)
perm
```

    Permutation Test:Transition Network (relative probabilities) [directed]
      Iterations: 1000  |  Alpha: 0.05
      Nodes: 9  |  Edges tested: 78  |  Significant: 42

``` r

splot(perm)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 11: Green = High \> Low, red = Low \> High (p \< 0.05)

``` r

splot(perm, show_nonsig = TRUE)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 12: All edges — significant solid, non-significant dashed

``` r

splot(perm, show_stars = TRUE, show_effect = TRUE)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 13: With significance stars and effect sizes

## 7 Motifs

Nestimate objects work directly with cograph’s motif analysis.
[`motifs()`](http://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/motifs.md) counts MAN
triad types;
[`subgraphs()`](http://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/subgraphs.md)
identifies specific node triples.

``` r

mot <- cograph::motifs(net, significance = TRUE, n_perm = 100, seed = 42)
mot
```

    Motif Census
    Level: aggregate | States: 9 | Pattern: triangle
    Significance: permutation (n_perm=100)

    Type distribution:

    210 300
      1   1

    Top 2 results:
     type count expected     z      p  sig
      300    77      6.3 21.25 0.0000 TRUE
      210     7     21.6 -2.30 0.0216 TRUE

``` r

plot(mot, type = "types")
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 14: Triad type distribution

``` r

plot(mot, type = "significance")
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 15: Over- and under-represented triad types

Named subgraphs — which states form which patterns:

``` r

sg <- cograph::subgraphs(net, significance = FALSE, top = 10)
sg
```

    NULL

``` r

plot(mot, type = "patterns")
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 16: MAN triad pattern diagrams

## 8 Higher-Order Networks

When first-order Markov models are insufficient, Nestimate detects
higher-order sequential dependencies.

### 8.1 HON

[`build_hon()`](https://rdrr.io/pkg/Nestimate/man/build_hon.html)
identifies transitions where prior context changes the outgoing
distribution:

``` r

hon <- build_hon(net)
hon
```

    Higher-Order Network (HON)
      Nodes:        719 (9 first-order states)
      Edges:        2855
      Max order:    5 (requested 5)
      Min freq:     1
      Trajectories: 2000

### 8.2 HYPA

[`build_hypa()`](https://rdrr.io/pkg/Nestimate/man/build_hypa.html)
detects paths that occur significantly more or less often than expected:

``` r

hypa <- build_hypa(net)
table(hypa$scores$anomaly)
```


    normal   over  under
      1921    546    117 

``` r

over <- hypa$scores[hypa$scores$anomaly == "over", ]
head(over[order(-over$ratio), c("path", "ratio", "observed", "expected")], 8)
```

## 9 The Dispatch Chain

Every Nestimate object routes through
[`splot()`](http://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/splot.md):

``` r

splot(net)      # netobject       → network plot
splot(boot)     # net_bootstrap   → stability-styled
splot(grp_net)  # netobject_group → multi-panel grid
splot(perm)     # net_permutation → difference network
```

All standard [`splot()`](http://sonsoles.me/cograph/reference/splot.md)
arguments (`layout`, `node_fill`, `edge_color`, `title`, etc.) work with
every object type.
